book_understanding.teaching_order: Follows a textbook order (rule, exceptions, classification bases, each class) but inserts small 'why' turns that a textbook leaves out: the reason for exemptions (no double regulator), the learner's objection about non-deposit NBFCs (then where does the money come from?), and why a housing lender serves businesses (small firms work from home). The activity types are a flat run of ten in a fixed rail order, each with the same 'next is NBFC X, yaani...' formula; only factoring and account aggregation get a story, placed at the point where the abstract label would fail.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Cut by the questions a regulator asks (must it register? does it take public deposits? what does it do?), then give each answer-class one short definition, and add a story only where the definition alone is not understood.

opening.what: Recalls the previous video (what an NBFC is and how it differs from banks), then moves straight to registration: RBI regulates NBFCs, so each must register with RBI.

narration.density: About 28 terms (registration, regulatory body, NHB, IRDA, SEBI, dual registration, classification, asset-liability structure, NBFC-D, NBFC-ND, ICC, hire purchase, IFC, IDF, debt securities, MFI, self-employment, HFC, MGC, mortgage guarantee, CIC-SI, core sectors, factoring, invoice, discount, P2P, commission, account aggregator) in about 460 s, about 3.6 per minute. The ten-type run (about 4.5 minutes, ten codes plus full forms) is too dense to remember from labels alone; the two stories slow it at the right places. Pace of voice (about 158 words a minute) is comfortable.

talmel_summary: The picture is a labelled index of the talk: almost every change is a name or a definition box that appears with, or 1-2 s before, the spoken name, so sync is good (13 together, 11 picture first, none late) but the relation is mostly 'writes the word' (9 name labels, 8 text boxes repeating speech). The picture carries meaning only twice: the 'Register' arrow from NBFC to RBI with its 'Exceptions' pill, and the '?' that sits on NBFC-ND while the learner's question is open. The two best spoken passages, the factoring story and the multi-account dashboard, get no drawing at all; the screen holds still for 35-40 s while actors and money move only in the voice.

voice.notes: About 158 words a minute, calm, steady, conversational. Each type follows one formula ('next hai NBFC X, yaani <full form>; ye NBFCs ... provide karati hain'), which helps recall but becomes monotonous over ten items. Objections are voiced with 'aap poochhoge' (twice) and stories begin with 'maan lijiye'; full forms are read in English. Stresses 'exception', 'dual registration', 'factoring'. About 14.5 s of speech (75.5-90 s) was not recognised by the transcript.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs company A, a small maker who has just delivered goods worth ₹1,00,000 to company B on a 60-day bill; wages of ₹60,000 are due in 10 days. Each day the player chooses: wait, or take the bill to an NBFC factor.
game_ideas.process_happens: The bill card travels to the NBFC, which pays A ₹97,000 at once (₹3,000 kept as discount); a calendar runs to day 60, when B pays the NBFC, not A. A's cash meter, wage due date and the NBFC's collection are all visible.
game_ideas.win: Wages paid on time, production keeps running, and the fee paid is the smallest needed (factor only the bills you must).
game_ideas.lose: Waiting: cash hits zero on day 10, workers stop, the next order is lost. Factoring every small bill: fees pile up and profit shrinks, shown as a growing fee stack.

game_ideas.player_does: Drags company cards (insurer, stock broker, mutual fund, merchant banker, nidhi company, chit fund, microfinance lender, P2P platform, consumer-loan company) to the regulator buildings that already watch them (RBI, IRDAI, SEBI, MCA, state government).
game_ideas.process_happens: Cards that land with a regulator other than RBI get an 'exempt from RBI registration' stamp; RBI-regulated cards get a 'Register' arrow to the RBI building.
game_ideas.win: Every card with the right regulator, and no card registered twice.
game_ideas.lose: Sending an insurer to RBI as well as IRDAI makes two inspectors arrive with two forms; the game names this 'dual registration' and asks which one to remove.
game_ideas.concept: exemptions: already-regulated companies, avoiding dual registration

game_ideas.player_does: Customers walk in with needs ('₹20,000 to start tailoring in my village', 'turn my unpaid bill into cash', 'a 15-year loan for a toll road', 'see all my accounts in one place', 'lend my savings to other people myself', 'a bank wants its home loans guaranteed') and the player sends each to a stop on the ten-type rail.
game_ideas.process_happens: The chosen NBFC acts: MFI gives a small loan, Factor buys the bill, IFC lends long-term, AA opens one dashboard, P2P matches a lender to a borrower, MGC stamps a guarantee.
game_ideas.win: All customers served by the right type within a time limit.
game_ideas.lose: A wrong match shows what that NBFC really does (P2P refuses to lend its own money; AA shows data but gives no cash), then the customer walks to the right stop.
game_ideas.concept: platform NBFCs: P2P and account aggregator

checks_learned: A spoken story longer than about 20 s with two or more actors and a transfer (A sells to B, NBFC pays A, NBFC collects from B) must have those actors and transfers drawn; a still canvas during such a story fails.
An on-screen list of N items where the voice covers fewer (nine exempt types, three spoken) must be cut to what is spoken, or every item must be spoken.
Real brand names (banks, broking apps) in examples are replaced by generic names before rendering.
Internal consistency: an entity shown as exempt from a regulator (housing finance companies) must not also appear as one of that regulator's categories without a line explaining the change.
Regulatory facts that changed over time (who regulates HFCs; the current list of NBFC types) need a dated source check before use.
A full form shown on screen (Infrastructure Debt Fund) must be spoken, or the code alone shown.
Definitions are checked against an authoritative glossary; a description that contradicts the usual definition (CIC-SI as 'investment in core sectors') blocks the scene.

When the voice asks the learner's question, a '?' is placed on the item in question and replaced by the answer when it is given (worked here at 144-163 s); enforce this pattern for every voiced objection.
A transcript gap over 10 s inside a run flags a dropped or garbled narration line (here about 75.5-90 s).

teaching_best.why: The learner's objection is voiced at the right moment (if ND cannot take deposits, how does it lend?), pinned with a '?' on the diagram, and answered in one line.
The exemption rule gets its reason (no point in a second regulator), which turns a list into a principle.
IFC and IDF are taught as one goal, two methods (lend directly vs buy the debt), which separates two look-alike codes.
A second voiced objection (why would a housing lender serve businesses?) is answered with an everyday fact (small firms work from home).
Factoring is taught as a small business story with a time delay, a cash crunch and a fee, which is what makes the term make sense.

teaching_weak.why: A nine-row English list of exempt companies stays on screen for about 80 s while only three are explained.
CIC-SI is described as investing in core sectors of the economy, which looks wrong; it is usually defined by holding investments in its own group companies.
HFCs are presented as NHB-regulated and exempt, then listed as an RBI NBFC type; likely dated and left unexplained.
The account aggregator example uses real bank and broker names.
No recap: ten types and two classification bases end with a one-line 'covered fully'.
